opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a long tradition in machine learning, and in AI evaluation more broadly, of trying to break capabilities down into small, well-defined pieces that you can measure cleanly. You pick some narrow skill, like answering a multiple-choice question, solving a short math problem, or completing a single function given a docstring. Then you build a dataset of lots of independent examples of that skill and report accuracy. The appeal is pretty clear. These tasks are cheap to run and easy to grade automatically. They're reproducible, and you can get tight error bars because you have thousands of samples. It feels very scientific: you control for confounders and isolate the variable you care about.

I think that approach has been really valuable, and benchmarks like that drove a lot of progress. But my view has shifted toward thinking it has some important limitations, especially if what you actually care about is how these systems will affect the world. The implicit assumption is that if you measure a bunch of atomic skills, you can sort of compose them and predict how a model will do on real, messy, long-horizon work. I'm not sure that assumption holds. A lot of what makes real tasks hard is the stuff that gets stripped out when you isolate things. That includes figuring out what the task even is, recovering from mistakes, and managing context over hours. It also includes dealing with ambiguous specifications and knowing when you're done.

There's also the saturation problem. These isolated tasks tend to get saturated really quickly, sometimes within a year or two of release. That makes it hard to track trends over time or say anything about where things are heading. And because the tasks are short and self-contained, it's often unclear how a given score maps onto anything you'd care about economically or from a safety perspective. Does 85% versus 90% on some QA benchmark mean anything for whether a model can do a week of an ML engineer's work? Usually it's pretty hard to say.

So the way I'd put it is that isolating simple tasks gives you precision, but at the cost of validity, meaning how well the measurement tracks the thing you actually want to know about. A lot of the work I've been thinking about is trying to move toward more holistic, realistic tasks, while keeping enough rigor that you can still draw real conclusions from them.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluations break capabilities into small, well-defined pieces to measure them cleanly, and explains that this isolates the variable being measured and improves precision.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that a lot of traditional benchmarking in machine learning comes from this tradition where you want to understand some specific capability in isolation. So you construct a dataset where each example tests one narrow thing: can the model answer this multiple choice question about biology, can it do this arithmetic problem, can it classify the sentiment of this sentence. And the appeal there is that it's really clean. You get a number, it's reproducible, it's cheap to run, and if performance goes up you have a pretty clear story about what changed.

And I think that approach has been genuinely useful. A lot of what we've learned about scaling, about how capabilities emerge, came from benchmarks like that. But I've become fairly skeptical that it tells you what you actually care about, which is, can this system do useful work in the world, or can it do dangerous things in the world. Because real tasks aren't isolated. They're long, they involve a bunch of sub-skills that have to be chained together, there's a lot of context you have to track, you have to recover from mistakes, you have to figure out what the task even is in a lot of cases. And when you decompose a task into simple pieces and test each piece, you lose all of that. You can have a model that does great on every individual component and still falls over when you ask it to do the whole thing.

The other thing is that simple tasks saturate really quickly now. You build a benchmark, it's hard for a year or two, and then models are at ninety-something percent and the remaining errors are mostly label noise. So you end up measuring the ceiling of your dataset instead of the model. That's part of why with GPQA we tried to go toward questions that are genuinely hard for experts, and then with the work at METR the move has been toward longer, more realistic tasks where you're actually watching an agent try to accomplish something over hours.

So I guess my overall view is that isolating simple tasks is a reasonable thing to do as one input, especially early on when you're trying to understand mechanisms. But as the central approach to measuring what these systems can do, I think it's increasingly misleading, and the field has been slow to update on that because the simple approach is so much more convenient.

r001.rationale: The response says isolated benchmarks test one narrow capability at a time, giving a clean, reproducible measure and a clear story about what changed. This conveys precise measurement of a task’s components as the rationale for isolating them.

astra-6.text:
I think the idea is to take some broader capability you care about and break it down into relatively simple tasks that you can measure in a controlled way. So instead of asking whether a model can do scientific research, you might ask whether it can answer a particular scientific question or identify a flaw in an experimental design. That makes it easier to score performance and understand what the model is actually succeeding or failing at.

The tricky part is relating those measurements back to the broader capability. Doing well on each of the individual tasks doesn’t necessarily mean the system can put them together, decide which ones to do, and carry out a long project. So I see these evaluations as useful pieces of evidence, but you have to be careful about what you infer from them.

r001.rationale: The response says to break a broader capability into simple tasks measured in a controlled way, making performance easier to score and showing what the model succeeds or fails at. This communicates the rationale of isolating tasks for more precise measurement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the idea is to take some capability that we care about and try to isolate it in a task where success or failure is relatively easy to interpret. So instead of asking whether a model can do an entire job, you ask whether it can perform particular pieces of that job. That gives you more controlled measurements, and it can help you understand where a system is struggling.

The difficulty is that those pieces don’t necessarily compose in the way you’d expect. A model might be able to do each step when you explicitly ask it to, but fail to recognize when to take those steps in a larger task. So I’d think of these measurements as useful evidence about capabilities, but not a complete account of what the system can accomplish in practice.

r001.rationale: The response says to break a job into particular pieces and measure those pieces in controlled tasks, explaining that their success or failure is easier to interpret.
